I feel why the insights from the experiment doesn't help that much, right? how do you think about it?

Yes, I agree. The main reason isn't bad analysis: the round 1 experiment was built to pick a winner, not to explain why messages work. No amount of analysis can pull more out of data than the experiment put in.

## 🧪 The data holds 13 points, not 444,691
1. **Built to rank**: round 1 compared 13 whole messages to see which one wins.
2. **Changes bundled**: each message differed from the others in greeting, sender, framing and length at once.
3. **No cause**: salience beats socialNorms by 11.76 points, and nothing says which difference did it.
4. **Wrong sample size**: for any question about wording, n = 13, as FI10 says.

Design needs to know why something works: does naming the doctor help, and does "ready for your review" beat "require"? You can only answer that when those features are varied one at a time. Round 1 never did that. So the ceiling on insight was set when the experiment was designed, before any Insight page was written.

## 🔁 Most pages answer the same thing again
1. **One real answer**: salience wins, and the designs already use it.
2. **Audience cuts**: the ~80 subgroup pages repeat one result, "no subgroup has a different winner".
3. **Questions from the data**: A00 copied the paper's 31 topics, not the questions a designer has.
4. **Craft isn't in the data**: the review fixes on ITEM06 were about writing and compliance.

Knowing "one winner, no flips" once is worth a lot. Deriving it again for five audiences adds pages, not knowledge. And some of what makes a good SMS was never going to come from click data at all. Examples are whether a colon ties the link to the right ask, or whether "may be able to save" promises too much.

## ⚖️ Where I'd push back a little
1. **Real value**: it gave the base (salience) and saved real work ("don't segment").
2. **The limits matter most**: knowing what's unknown, like the sender, shows what to test next.
3. **About five pages**: that's a small yield from the data, not a sign the method failed.

So I wouldn't call the insights useless. They're the right answers to the experiment's own question, "which of these 13 should we send?", and that answer fits on one page. The mistake was expecting them to guide new wording, which this experiment can't support.

## 💡 What would make insight useful next time
1. **Design the send to teach**: vary a few features across arms, like FW02 W1 says.
2. **Example**: greeting on/off × "require" vs "ready for your review" × doctor named or not = 8 messages.
3. **Then analyze**: each Insight page asks "did this feature help?", and each answer changes the next draft.
4. **Why questions**: published SMS-reminder trials, brought in through `haipipe-discovery`, cover what one send can't.

The loop should run: design question → a send built to answer it → insight → next design. Right now it runs backwards: analyze old messages, then design. If you want, I can draft that 8-message round-2 set for all patients, each with a `because: FW02 · W1` line, as the first insight-driven Design folder.
What is the value of the insight's from the previous online experiments?

Their value is in decisions and baselines, not in wording. They tell you what to send now, what not to spend effort on, what is still unknown, and what numbers the next experiment has to beat. They can't tell you how to write a better message.

## ✅ What they're worth
1. **Choice already made**: send salience to everyone; it won on both clicks and sign-ins.
2. **Work avoided**: no separate messages per audience; no subgroup had a different winner.
3. **Claims blocked**: no rule scores an untested message, so no one can promise a lift.
4. **Baselines**: salience's 66.06% click rate is the number round 2 has to beat.
5. **Drop-off found**: clickers are lost at the identity check, a step worth designing for.

The first three avoid bad decisions, and that's worth a lot. Without them the team would likely have shipped several of the paper's 20 proposed messages (none was supported), or kept six audience versions of every message. The baselines matter for planning the next send: they give the rate to beat, the size of a gap worth detecting (salience beat socialNorms by 11.76 points), and so how many sends each new arm needs.

## 🧭 What they point to next
1. **Known unknowns**: the sender was never varied, and nobody knows why salience wins.
2. **Next test**: vary a few features at once instead of adding whole new messages (FW02 W1).
3. **Skip**: spend no arms separating the middle nine messages; that answer isn't worth the cost.

This part is easy to undervalue. A clear list of what the data can't answer tells you exactly what to test next. Most of round 2's useful designs, the sender tests and the identity-check notice, come from these gaps, not from positive findings.

## ❌ What they can't give
1. **Wording**: no insight says which phrase, tone or framing works better.
2. **Mechanism**: each message changed several things at once, so no cause can be isolated.
3. **New winners**: they can't predict how a message that was never sent will do.

## 💡 In one line
1. **Worth**: about five decisions and a set of baselines; that's the payoff.
2. **Not worth**: 115 pages; most of them repeat the same few answers.

Going forward, the real value comes from treating the next send as the source of insight. Build it so each result names a cause, and then the insight pages will guide wording in a way round 1 never could.

I am still thinking what is the design method, what is the general method of designing,

for the design what is the desing input, what is hte design processing ,and what is the design output?

Do you get what I mean here?

Yes, I think I get it. You're asking what the design method looks like in general, independent of SMS and of our tooling: what goes in, what happens in the middle, and what comes out. Here's how I'd frame it, and where our current system fits and falls short.

## 🧩 The general design method
1. **Input**: a goal, what we already know, and the constraints.
2. **Processing**: choose what to vary, generate options, check them, pick one.
3. **Output**: the design, the reason for it, and a prediction you can test.
4. **Loop**: the test result becomes input for the next round.

```
INPUT                    PROCESSING                       OUTPUT
goal (who, what action)  1 frame the problem              the design (the text)
knowledge (what works)   2 choose design variables        the reason (which rule / idea)
constraints (rules)      3 generate options               the bet (expected / wrong if)
base design              4 check against rules
                         5 select
        ▲                                                       │
        └──────────── learning from the send ◄──────────────────┘
```

## 📥 Input: four kinds
1. **Goal**: who it's for, the one action we want, the channel (Brief).
2. **Knowledge**: what's known to work, from data, theory or published trials (Insight).
3. **Constraints**: length, opt-out wording, no health details, compliance.
4. **Starting point**: a base design to change, such as salience.

Knowledge is the weakest input today. Last round it came mostly from one experiment that ranked 13 messages, so it could say "start from salience" but not "why".

## ⚙️ Processing: the step we skip is choosing variables
1. **Frame**: what problem does this message have to solve for the reader?
2. **Variables**: name what can change, such as sender, greeting, framing and the reason to act.
3. **Generate**: write options that change one or a few variables.
4. **Check**: does each option meet the rules? (our Verify)
5. **Select**: which ones go out?

Step 2 is the heart of the method, and our system has no place for it. Today each Design Item is a whole idea written freely, so the variables stay hidden inside the wording. That's the same flaw round 1 had. If the variables are named first, every design says what it changes, and the result tells you which change mattered.

## 📤 Output: a design is also a question
1. **Artifact**: the message itself (our Delivery).
2. **Rationale**: why this design; the `because:` line I just added.
3. **Bet**: what it should do and what would prove it wrong (`expected` / `falsified`).
4. **After sending**: the result, which feeds the next round's knowledge.

Verify only judges quality, meaning the design follows the rules. Only the send can judge whether it works. So a design's real output isn't finished until the result comes back and is written down as knowledge.

## 🗺️ Where our system stands
1. **Have**: goal (Brief), knowledge (Insight board), rules and bet (register), generate and check (Runs), artifact (Delivery).
2. **Missing**: an explicit design-variable step between the goal and the drafts.
3. **Missing**: the loop from send results back into knowledge.

Is this the level you mean, the method in general, before we decide how the tool should support it? If so, the next step I'd suggest is writing it up as a short one-page Design Method (input, processing, output, loop) and checking the SMS work against it.

As long as they are the paper's 31 topics repeated for six audiences, the new view will just show the same thin answers more clearly.

## ✅ What the Insight session got right
1. **Logic left, work right**: the questions at each level on the left, the runs that answer them on the right.
2. **Runs give the answer**: FD03 and FI02 only restated their CSVs, so dropping those pages loses nothing.
3. **One dataset per workbench**: SMSR2v1 is A00 and SMSR3Full is A03; comparing rounds means comparing workbenches.
4. **No codes on screen**: "Knowledge question 2", not QK2.
5. **It noticed what's missing**: nothing records an expected answer, so the board can only accept or refuse.

Point 2 removes most of the overbuilding we found in A00. Point 5 is the same weakness we found from the Design side, seen from the other end.

## 🔄 What I'd change: questions come from Design
1. **Input today**: a dataset plus questions copied from a paper.
2. **Input I'd want**: a dataset plus questions from Design ("does naming the doctor help?").
3. **Expected answer**: each Design Item's `expected` / `falsified` is the prior Insight is missing.
4. **Output**: answers Design can cite by id, such as `because: FW02 · W1`.

This fits the design method from my last message:

```
Design (B00)                          Insight (A03, next dataset)
item + design variable + bet   ──►    question: "did ITEM03 beat salience?"
        ▲                             prior   = the item's expected
        │                             work    = runs on the new send's data
        └──── because: <answer id> ◄── answer + was the bet right?
```

Round 3 already gives a test case. efficiencyTech beat salience by 3.1 points, and A00 had called it unwarranted. With priors written down, A03 could score that directly: A00 said no, and the send said yes. That is the calibration and bet-yield scoring the Insight session proposed, and Design's registers already hold half of what it needs.

## ⚠️ Two cautions about the new view
1. **Seven partition tables**: in A00 almost every audience cut ended at "no different winner", so most rows will be greyed.
2. **My suggestion**: open on Full; show another partition only where its answer differs.
3. **IDs Design depends on**: my new `because:` line reads W rows from page files.
4. **If W answers become `answer.md` in the result store**: the Design lookup and the signed-handoff check both have to read from there.

Point 3 is a real coordination risk. If the Insight session drops pages without a stable answer id and location, every `because:` line and B00's insight eligibility check break at once. That needs one agreed contract: where an answer lives, what its id is (for example `FW02 · W1`), and how a sign-off is recorded.

1. **Not touching `insightboard.py`**: the Insight session is rewriting it right now.
2. **Agree the contract first**: answer id, its location, its sign-off, and its link back to a Design Item.
3. **Then the Design side**: `because:` reads answers from that location, keeping page files as a fallback for A00.
4. **Next board, not A00**: build Design-driven questions on A03 (round 3 data) and leave A00 as history.

2. **Goal**: the Brief line (who, their job, the venue, how many) plus the fixed rules.

The core view is the Design table. The Logic side groups designs by the one variable each changes ("Sender designs · messenger effect"). Under each design it shows the rule it follows (`because`), its theory and its bet. The Work side shows Commission → Generate → Verify and the draft. Clicking a design opens its history in a pop-out. For Design 6 that's the failed rd22 review and the final 136-character SMS. The screen says "Design 3", while the files keep ITEM03.

1. **13 common theories**: salience, messenger effect, goal gradient, ease, reason ("because"), framing, social norms and others.
2. **Columns for each**: what it says, the variable it moves, its EAST group, its round-1 arm, its B00 design and its source.
3. **Anatomy of one SMS**: Design 5 cut into greeting, sender, next step, lead and ask, each matched to its theory.
4. **Method loop**: Goal → Knowledge → pick one variable → design → bet → Verify → send → Insight → back to Knowledge.

The most useful finding came from building this. All 13 round-1 arms were named after these theories, so round 1 was already a theory bake-off. But each arm rewrote the whole message, so it tested 13 messages, not 13 theories. That's why no theory was confirmed or ruled out. The drawing makes the rule explicit: a theory helps a design only when the design changes the one variable that theory names.

## 🧠 The design theory you described
1. **Design is abduction**: you know only the value you want; you must create both the "what" and the "how" (Dorst 2011).
2. **Not selection**: choosing from a set is the easy part; round 1 treated design as picking 1 of 13.
3. **C-K theory**: a new design can't be judged with today's knowledge; only a test settles it, and the result becomes new knowledge (Hatchuel & Weil 2003).
4. **Satisficing**: aim for good enough within the constraints, never provably best (Simon 1969).

Part 4 of the drawing makes this the backbone, in four panels:
- **The design problem**: deduction, induction, choosing and designing, side by side. Insight explains; design creates.
- **Inputs, process, output**:
  - In: aim, constraints and resources.
  - Steps: frame → generate → predict → check → choose → test.
  - Out: the design, its rationale, its bet, the test plan, and new knowledge fed back.
- **Theory behind each step**:
  - framing: Schön; Dorst & Cross
  - generating: C-K; Zwicky's morphological analysis
  - one variable at a time: Suh's axiomatic design
  - predicting: Gero's function-behaviour-structure
  - choosing: Simon; set-based design
  - process: Double Diamond; wicked problems
- **What to attend to, and what not to**:
  - Attend to: the value, the frame, the variables, hard constraints, options that differ in principle, and a prediction written before the test.
  - Avoid: picking only among what was tried before, treating a prediction as knowledge, and gathering knowledge that changes no design.

Message theories like salience and the messenger effect are now part 5. They're one kind of resource, under Knowledge › Theory. As before, I listed the sources from memory; they should be checked before anyone cites them.

   - generating: C-K theory; Zwicky
   - one variable at a time: Suh
   - predicting: Gero
   - choosing: Simon; set-based design
   - process: Double Diamond; Rittel & Webber

## 🧭 The Design Process, Forward
1. **Control**: start from the tested message, salience as sent
2. **Slots**: split the message into its parts: sender, content, context, ask, link, opt-out
3. **Frame**: pick the one slot to change, and the theory that predicts it helps
4. **Allow**: name the Wisdom row that permits the change; every other slot stays fixed
5. **Realize, check**: write the words; Verify checks each part against its claim

This logic is already written down in our own materials but not wired in. The SMS venue's template gives each slot a `claim_source`, meaning each part of a message must name what backs it. And the board's Theory of Design says: "A theory helps a design only when the design changes the one variable that theory names and keeps the rest fixed against a control (salience)." It also names the variable each theory moves: Expectedness moves the context, Messenger effect the sender, Goal gradient the frame, Processing fluency the words and length.

So the rationale should be made at three moments, and each one writes its own piece:

| Step | Who | Writes | On the card |
|---|---|---|---|
| Design Goal | you, with the agent | the control text, the slots, the rules | what every design is read against |
| Commission | you sign | the changed slot, its theory, the allowing row | the bet, before any words exist |
| Generate | designer agent | words per slot, why, source (`rationale.yaml`) | Design decisions |
| Verify | a fresh reviewer | each claim checked against its source | ✓ per decision, Review notes |
| Workbench | reads only | nothing | the evidence behind a cited row |

## 📚 Classical Design Methods
1. **Eight methods**: each comes from a design theory, read here as an AI skill
2. **A ladder**: each reads more before it designs, from goal only to goal plus insights
3. **Ready on this board**: all except reader test have their inputs already

| Method | Theory it comes from | AI reads | AI returns |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 · By goal | Dorst 2011, normal problem solving; Simon 1969 | the Design Goal | the SMS |
| 2 · By principle | Schön 1983, reflection-in-action; Dorst 2015, frame creation | the Design Goal | the SMS, its frame and reasons |
| 3 · By slots | Zwicky 1969, morphological box; Suh 1990, axiomatic design | the goal plus the message's slots | options per slot, one slot changed |
| 4 · By theory | Bartholomew 1998, Intervention Mapping; Michie 2011, Behaviour Change Wheel | the goal plus the Theory of Design | the SMS, its mechanism, variable and prediction |
| 5 · By insight | Sackett 1996, evidence-based practice | the goal plus signed insight rows | the SMS, one cited decision per slot |
| 6 · By precedent | Kolodner 1993, case-based reasoning; Alexander 1977, pattern language | the goal plus past designs | the SMS, the case it adapted, and how |
| 7 · By reader test | ISO 9241-210, human-centred design; Ericsson & Simon 1993, think-aloud | the goal plus reader profiles | the SMS, what readers did each round |
| 8 · By exploring | Sobek 1999, set-based design; Holland 1975, evolutionary search | the goal, plus any of the above | several SMS, each naming its try |

Method 4 is the standard way health communication designs messages: a theory picks a determinant, the determinant picks a technique, and the technique picks the words. Method 3 fits what our insight board already advises: W02's row W1 says to vary two or three features across many arms. Method 6 has material on this board already: the 13 round-1 arms and Gen 1's twenty messages. Method 7 needs reader profiles. Using AI to stand in for readers is cheap, but whether it predicts real readers is unproven.

## 🧪 How Each Is Tested
1. **A test ladder**: T0 to T4, cheap and now, up to costly and at the send
2. **Every method**: gets T0, the rules
3. **Claims bring T1**: a method that claims a reason is checked on it
4. **The method itself is a bet**: design one task by every method and compare

| Test | Asks | When | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0 · Rules | keeps every constraint and acceptance rule | now, Verify | verification (Boehm 1984) |
| T1 · Fidelity | does what its method claims: technique present, row cited right | now, Verify | |
| T2 · Critique | an independent expert reads it | now, Review notes | Nielsen & Molich 1990 |
| T3 · Pretest | readers understand it, trust it, would act | before the send | Dillard et al. 2007 |
| T4 · Field | a randomized send against the control | at the send | validation |

Which methods need which tests:

1. **By goal:** T0 only.
2. **By principle:** T0 plus T2 on its frame.
3. **By slots:** T1 (only one slot changed), and later a T4 factorial test.
4. **By theory:** T1 (is the named technique really in the text?), plus a T3 pretest.
5. **By insight:** T1 on every cited row.
6. **By precedent:** T1 (not a copy of the case), and later T4 against that case.
7. **By reader test:** T3 is built into the method.
8. **By exploring:** T0 on each candidate, T2 to rank them, T4 to choose.

O'Cathain's eight categories are:

1. **Partnership:** the people who will use the intervention decide with the team.
2. **Target population-centred:** built on users' views and actions.
3. **Evidence and theory-based:** built on published evidence and existing theory.
4. **Implementation-based:** built so it will be used in the real world.
5. **Efficiency-based:** components tested experimentally to keep the ones that work.
6. **Stepped or phased:** a fixed sequence of steps.
7. **Intervention-specific:** made for one type of intervention.
8. **Combination:** existing approaches formally combined.

## 💡 My Thoughts
1. **Use O'Cathain as the backbone**: it's a peer-reviewed taxonomy of exactly "same aim, different ways"
2. **Three of its categories don't fit**: partnership and implementation need people; stepped is our pipeline
3. **The method comparison is the gap**: no review compares methods head to head for SMS
4. **Theory needs a fidelity check**: Prestwich shows a named theory alone predicts nothing
5. **Exploring needs forced spread**: Doshi & Hauser show AI designs drift together

Prestwich and Doshi & Hauser change how two methods should be built. By theory must prove the technique is actually in the text (our T1 fidelity test), or naming a theory is decoration. By exploring must require candidates to differ in principle, not just in wording, because an AI left alone converges.

Hölbling 2025 makes method 1 an honest baseline rather than a straw man. AI messages written straight from the goal already persuade about as well as human ones. So the richer methods have to beat a good control, not a weak one.

## 📘 What the Two MISQ Papers Are About
1. **Not intervention design**: both are about design science research in IS
2. **Their "design"**: building and evaluating an IT artifact as a way of doing research
3. **What they give us**: how a design counts as a contribution in a UTD24 IS paper
4. **The fit**: our design method, not one SMS, would be the contribution they describe

Hevner et al. 2004 says design science builds and evaluates IT artifacts of four kinds: constructs, models, methods and instantiations. Gregor & Hevner 2013 is about the level of abstraction a design study contributes (its abstract says so). In practice the levels run from one working instance, through design principles, up to a fuller design theory.

Read that way, one SMS is only an instance. The AI design methods and the workbench are the method, and that's the part an IS journal would count as the contribution. So the two papers frame how our work would be judged, not how to design an intervention. Intervention design is O'Cathain, MRC 2021, Intervention Mapping and the Behaviour Change Wheel, all health journals.

Taxonomy of approaches to developing interventions to improve health: a systematic methods overview

This paper is most relevant, right?
I'll check the full text quickly before answering, since its PDF is now saved.

Yes. For the theory of design methods, it's the single most relevant paper. It's the one review that shows a single design task can be approached by distinct, named methods, and our eight methods map onto its taxonomy. But it only maps the methods; it doesn't say which one works better.

## 🎯 Why it's the anchor
1. **Same question as ours**: what different ways exist to develop one intervention
2. **Eight categories**: partnership, population-centred, evidence and theory, implementation, efficiency, stepped, specific, combination
3. **Maps onto our methods**: four of our eight methods line up with its categories
4. **Shared actions**: 18 actions common to all approaches, like our shared loop
5. **PDF inside**: it's the first card under All methods, with a PDF badge

It's a systematic methods overview of published approaches to developing health interventions: books, websites or articles after 2007, or approaches cited by intervention studies from 2015 to 2016. That matches our framing of one design task with several possible methods.

The mapping, already in `design-methods.md`:
- **By theory and By insight**: its evidence and theory-based approach
- **By user test**: its target population-centred approach
- **By slots**: its efficiency-based approach (component testing, as in Collins 2018)
- **Our shared loop**: its stepped or phased approach

Its partnership and implementation-based approaches need people at every step, which our AI-run process doesn't model.

## ⚠️ What it does not give us
1. **No head-to-head**: "Authors did not formally compare their approach with others"
2. **No quality ranking**: no appraisal of approaches, "because assessment criteria do not exist"
3. **Human teams, 2019**: about research teams developing health interventions, not AI

From the full text: each approach's strengths and limits are mostly reported by its own authors. So it supports "the methods exist and differ", not "method X beats method Y". That gap is what our `design-methods.md` calls the bet: design one task by several methods and compare them.

Other papers carry the claims it can't:
- **By goal as a strong baseline**: Hölbling 2025
- **Parallel designs beat serial ones**: Dow 2010
- **AI makes designs more alike**: Doshi & Hauser 2024
- **Naming a theory predicts nothing without a fidelity check**: Prestwich 2013
- **How a method counts as a research contribution**: Hevner 2004, Gregor & Hevner 2013

The "Applied to AI" side has seven fields:
- **The agent**: what it reads before designing.
- **Steps**: the agent's procedure.
- **Returns**: what it writes with the design.
- **Verify**: how a second agent tests the design.

## 🤖 Applied to AI, one line per method

| method | what the AI does | AI risk, and its check |
|---|---|---|
| 1 By goal | writes the design from the goal alone; the baseline every other method must beat | designs come out alike [Doshi & Hauser 2024]; no reason to check |
| 2 By principle | writes the frame first and freezes it, then designs to it | a frame invented after the fact; T2 critique of the frame |
| 3 By slots | splits the starting text into slots, lists options, changes one slot | slots that interact; the factorial test (T4) shows it |
| 4 By theory | picks a theory and technique code from a closed list | names a theory it does not use [Prestwich 2013]; blind T1 coding |
| 5 By insight | cites a signed insight row for each element of the design | a cited row that does not say it; T1, our current evidence chain |

## 📖 What the paper does
1. **Scope**: approaches to developing health interventions, published after 2007
2. **Taxonomy**: eight categories, sorted by the reason each approach's authors give
3. **Table 2**: each approach's rationale, context, steps, strengths and limitations, with sources
4. **18 actions**: grouped into seven domains, from Conception to Planning for evaluation
5. **Choosing**: six questions, including intention, context, values, skills, track record and resources

The seven domains are Conception, Planning, Designing, Creating, Refining, Documenting, and Planning for future evaluation. The authors' own judgments carry an "(INDEX)" tag, which is where our "(ours)" comes from. They separate "development" (the whole process) from "design" (the point where content, format and delivery are decided). Our methods mostly cover that design point plus the refining after it.

## 🤔 What I think of it
1. **Best map**: the broadest synthesis of approaches, with a reusable structure
2. **Honest limits**: no comparison of success, and no quality criteria
3. **Strengths are self-reported**: claims of effectiveness come from each approach's own authors
4. **Different axis**: it sorts by an approach's stated reason; we sort by what the designer reads
5. **Pre-AI**: every approach assumes human teams; none develops from the goal alone

For us the paper does four things:
- **Confirms the gap**: the authors state "a comparison of the success of each approach has not been undertaken". Comparing methods on one task is the open question, so our pilot answers something new.
- **Names what an AI-only process can't do**: partnership (the people the design is for share every decision) and implementation-based planning. I now say why they have no card.
- **Maps onto our shared loop**:
  - The Design Goal covers Conception and Planning.
  - Frame and Generate cover Designing and Creating.
  - The test now is Refining.
  - Delivery is Documenting.
  - The test in use is Planning for future evaluation.
- **Points at our field test**: its efficiency-based category includes micro-randomised trials, which is the shape of an SMS field test. That paper (Klasnja 2015) isn't in our list yet.

## 👥 Not limited to AI
1. **The framework is general**: the four families describe any designer, human or AI

## 📡 What "From use" means
1. **When**: after the design is sent, in normal operation, to real people at full scale
2. **What it reads**: real responses, such as replies, clicks, opt-outs and refills
3. **What changes**: the design itself keeps changing while it runs
4. **By adapting**: send several versions, then shift sends toward the ones that work
5. **By tailoring**: learn which version, wording or timing works for each person

For example, you send three wordings of a refill reminder. Each day, more sends go to the wording that's getting more refills, while a few still go to the others in case the early lead was luck. That's a multi-armed bandit, which Schwartz et al. 2017 ran on 750 million ad impressions.

This differs from the field test (T4). T4 judges one fixed design once, against a control, so an approved design stays the same in use. Under From use, the field test and the design are the same process, and real behaviour keeps reshaping the design.

Three is enough on one axis, and design theory backs it: the three families match the three kinds of reasoning in design. But there are other ways to sort the same methods, and each card could carry those as well.

## 🧠 Why three: the three kinds of design reasoning
1. **From the goal ↔ abduction**: only the value is known, so the AI must create both the what and the how
2. **From what is known ↔ deduction**: a known how (theory, rule, past case) predicts the result, and the AI applies it
3. **From testing drafts ↔ induction**: from what was tried and what happened, the AI learns the how
4. **Already on our Design theory page**: Dorst 2011's table, after Peirce: deduction, induction, abduction

Our Design theory page sets out the reasoning table:

```
           you know          you look for
Deduction  what + how        the result
Induction  what + result     the how
Abduction  result + how      the what
Design     the result        the what AND the how
```

From the goal is that last row. Kolko 2010 (*Design Issues*, verified) calls abduction the driver of design synthesis.

It also fits your point about results from use. The InsightBoard does the induction: from what was sent and what happened, it explains what worked. By insight then applies those signed rows deductively. That's why past results land in From what is known.

Peirce held there are only three kinds of inference, and that's the strongest reason three families isn't arbitrary. By precedent is reasoning by analogy, which some treat as a fourth kind. It sits with deduction here, because the past case is applied to the new goal.

## 🧭 Other axes the same methods can be sorted on
1. **Who takes part**: AI alone · a critic checks · readers react · people decide
2. **How many designs at once**: one · one slot changed · several in parallel
3. **Divergent or convergent**: open up options, or narrow to one
4. **When the evidence arrives**: before designing · while designing · after sending, for the next round
5. **Process stage**: O'Cathain's seven domains, from Conception to Planning for evaluation

"Who takes part" comes from Sanders & Stappers 2008 (*CoDesign*, verified, abstract read). Their map runs from the user as a subject, someone designed for, to the user as a partner, someone who designs with you. O'Cathain makes the same split: target population-centred versus partnership. "How many designs at once" is Dow 2010, Sobek 1999 and Loch 2001, all already in our list. "Divergent then convergent" is in O'Cathain's synthesis of the digital approaches.

Here are the eleven methods on three of these axes (By tailoring as proposed):

| method | reasoning | who takes part | designs at once |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 By goal | abduction | AI alone | one |
| 2 By principle | abduction | AI alone, a critic checks the frame | one |
| 3 By slots | abduction, combinatorial | AI alone | one slot changed |
| 4 By theory | deduction | AI alone, a blind coder checks | one |
| 5 By insight | deduction from induced knowledge | AI alone | one |
| 6 By precedent | analogy | AI alone | one, from a case |
| 7 By implementation | deduction | AI alone, reads the delivery setting | one |
| 8 By tailoring | deduction, per person | AI alone | one per reader |
| 9 By user test | induction | readers react | one, in rounds |
| 10 By exploring | induction, by comparison | critics rank | several in parallel |
| 11 By co-design | induction | people decide | several, people choose |

Read down the "who takes part" column, and the human role grows only in the last three. Read down "designs at once", and only By exploring and By co-design work with several designs in parallel. Dow 2010 and Doshi & Hauser 2024 suggest that matters for an AI designer.

## 🧠 The three reasoning types
1. **Deduction**: you know the what and the how; you predict the result
2. **Induction**: you know the what and the result; you learn the how
3. **Abduction**: you know the result; you propose the what, and sometimes the how too
4. **Two kinds of abduction**: Dorst 2011 splits it into abduction-1 and abduction-2

The split works like this:
- **Abduction-1**: the value and the how are known, so only the what is found. That's ordinary problem solving: a theory says what works, and you build the thing that applies it.
- **Abduction-2**: only the value is known, so both the what and the how must be found. Dorst calls this design abduction. Our page wrote "Design" in that row, which made it look like a fourth reasoning type.

So the table should say four rows, three types:

```

Deduction      what + how        the result
Induction      what + result     the how
Abduction-1    result + how      the what
Abduction-2    the result        the what AND the how

## 🧠 The reasoning types, more fully
1. **Deduction, induction, abduction**: Peirce's three kinds of inference; every argument is one of these
2. **Analogy**: reasoning from a similar past case; often counted separately (By precedent)
3. **Updating**: revising what you believe when new evidence arrives, the statistical form of induction
4. **Chains**: real methods string the types together, and "learn, then update" is a chain

"Learn from a previous experiment, then update" is two steps:
1. **Induction**: from what was sent and what happened, learn the how (which wording moved refills, and for whom).
2. **Abduction-1**: with that how now known, change the design to apply it.

That two-step chain is the loop itself, run from one round to the next. R1 led to R2 that way, and R2 to the designs this board is making.

## 🔁 Your case as a method: By revising

| method | what it reads | what it's for |
|---|---|---|
| By insight | signed rows, general lessons across many designs | any new design |
| By precedent | the closest past design | a new goal |
| **By revising** | **this design's own experiment result** | **the same goal, next round** |

By revising is narrower than both:
- **Its evidence**: what happened to this design, not a general lesson.
- **Its target**: the next version of the same design, not a new goal.

It returns the revised design, what changed, and which result each change answers. Verify (T1) then checks that each change really follows from the result it cites.

There's support for this already:
- **In the literature**: iterative design, "modify, test, modify again" (Gould & Lewis 1985); MOST's continuous cycle of optimisation and evaluation (O'Cathain 2019); sequential testing that learns between tests (Loch 2001).
- **In our workbench**: a revise Generate run already exists, taking a base design and feedback. By revising is that run, with the experiment's result as the feedback.

By adapting is the same idea run continuously. A bandit updates which version gets sent every day, rather than revising the wording between rounds. That's why I placed it under the field test: it updates the allocation, not the design.

## 🔁 The format with reasoning
1. **Induction**: Previous Exp → Design; learn what works from the results

The terms come from Dorst 2011, which uses three words:
- **what**: the message.
- **how**: the working principle, for example "a provider's name raises clicks".
- **result**: the outcome, a click.

Each reasoning type starts from two of these, or one, and finds the rest:
- **Induction**: what + result → how.
- **Abduction-1**: how + result → what.
- **Abduction-2**: result only → how + what.
- **Deduction**: what + how → predicted result.

In the workbench:
- The induction arrow is the InsightBoard.

1. **Two abductions**: the how is invented or brought in; no results read

## 🗂️ Kinds of previous data
1. **Experimental**: past messages with their results; shows what works

- **Experimental data**: gives a how for everyone, for example "a provider's name raises clicks".
- **Personal data**: gives a how for one reader, for example "this patient refills late and reads texts in the evening".

## 🧠 Where reasoning sits
1. **Requirements**: given, not inferred; they set the target result and the limits
2. **Insights**: supply the "how"; ours come from our induction, external ones from others'
3. **Design**: abduction; requirements + insights → message
4. **Tests**: deduction; T0 checks the requirements, and the Exp measures the goal

In Dorst's terms:
- **The requirements** are the result we want, plus its limits.
- **An insight** is the how.
- **The message** is the what.

With no insight, Design is abduction-2: it has to invent the how. With an insight, it is abduction-1: it only finds the what.

Requirements come in two kinds:
- **Hard limits**, such as a length cap or a required sender name: checked by T0 before anything is sent.
- **The goal**, such as more refills: only the Exp can measure it.

1. **Requirements always**: every method reads them, so they don't define a family
2. **Insight source**: families differ in which insights they read or produce
3. **Reasoning follows**: each insight source fixes the reasoning type
4. **Mixing allowed**: a card can read both; its family is its main source

|---|---|---|---|
| **From requirements only** | nothing | abduction-2 | By goal · By principle |
| **With external insights** | literature, theory | abduction-1, on others' induction | By theory · By implementation |

| **Making internal insights now** | data gathered during Design | induction in small loops | By user test · By co-design |
| **Making internal insights next** | nothing extra; sends several options | leaves the induction to the Exp | By exploring · By slots |

1. **"Evaluation" alone**: the card's Evaluation column already covers both stages

4. **Section 3**: "How a design is evaluated"

This matches the card's Evaluation column, which already splits into now and at the send. It's also the standard split in the evaluation literature (Scriven 1967): formative evaluation improves a design while it is being made, and summative evaluation judges the finished one. 2. **Verification loop / Validation loop**: built right versus the right design (Boehm 1984)

4. **Formative / Summative**: the evaluation literature's terms (Scriven 1967); the outer loop is formative too

Hevner 2007's three cycles fit our format almost exactly:
- **Design cycle**: the inner build-and-evaluate loop.
- **Relevance cycle**: requirements come in from the setting, and field tests go back out to it. That's our design requirements, the Exp, and the internal insights it produces.
- **Rigor cycle**: grounding comes in from the knowledge base and new knowledge goes back. That's our external insights.

The names are less plain than Revise and Learning, though, and the paper isn't a Paper Run yet. I'd cite it as the source of the plain names.

"Internal / External evaluation" would be confusing on our page, because internal insights come out of the Exp. The page would then say that internal insights come from the external evaluation.

| **Evaluate** | rules checked on the whole text | each rule and citation checked on its own element |
| **Exp** | one result per design | designs that differ in known elements → an effect per element |

| **Library** | none | every element ever used, with an id (slot + variant), its designs, sources and results |
